Auditing the Merkle proofs

Thirteen steps for checking that the Hax → DyLean proofs about Merkle trees say what is claimed of the Rust. Part I is the inclusion of one item. Part II is an ordered read under a checkpoint root. Wherever one piece of code must agree with another, both are shown side by side with what links them.

The proofs live on branch verify/qmdb-hax-dylean, in the checkout that holds this page. qmdb/README.md states the results of part I and qmdb/mmb/README.md those of part II; this guide is for the person who checks them. It is written for a reader who knows Rust and Merkle trees and has not used Lean or DyLean. No step asks you to read a proof.

Production baseline: b45ef2d78ea7535d8a51588912ba1e13e461b146. The panels and tables marked as generated are built from the sources by verification/audit/build.py, and check.sh fails when they are stale.

Out of scope: the hax pipeline. This audit assumes that hax, Charon and Aeneas translate the Rust faithfully into Lean, and that their models of the Rust core library match Rust. It does not audit them. Step 4 only checks how the pipeline is used: which tools are pinned, that regenerating the Lean reproduces the committed files, and that nothing was filled in by hand. A translation bug that changes the meaning of the verifier would leave every theorem here true of the wrong program.

Part I · Inclusion of one itemPart II · Ordered reads under a checkpoint root
What is provedTwo openings accepted at one location under one root carry the same item. Every acceptance that a client logs names the item stored there.A claim that a key has a value, or has none, that is accepted under a root equals what replaying the journal gives.
Root formatThis branch’s, with its domain bytes. One peak. The height of the tree is trusted.v2026.11.0’s, with the domain bytes of an MMB. Any number of peaks. The leaf count and the inactive-peak count come from the proof, and the root fixes them.
Verifier in the statementsinclusion::verify_element_inclusion: Rust written for the proof and extracted by hax.Production’s rules::verify_operation, extracted unchanged and proved to refine RawProof.verify, a Lean definition of the reader’s check.
Tie to the deployed verifierDifferential tests against production (L2).A refinement proof (M5), with production’s callers delegating to the extracted files (M3).
The attackerDyLean traces: the attacker sends any message it can derive.No trace. The statements hold for any proof and any root.
What is assumed of the databaseA root with an accepted opening for every stored item.The writer’s invariants: activity bits, successor links, the commit floor and the layout of the root.

Scope and assumptions

In scope: the Merkle target of the Hax → DyLean experiment, in two parts. For part I that is the production files it shares with the proof, the verification-only client, the handwritten Lean that states what the Rust means, the application assumption, the protocol model, the theorem statements and the checks that a machine runs. For part II it is the specification of an ordered read, the production files proved to refine it, what it assumes of the writer, and its checks. The BLS and SAKE targets are out of scope; they share steps 4 to 7. So is the proof that a consumer builds on part II: no statement here says what a checkpoint is or who authenticates it.

Four things are assumed and not audited. For each, the audit still checks how the proof depends on it.

#Assumed, not auditedWhat the audit still checksStep
A1hax, Charon and Aeneas translate the Rust faithfully. Their models of the Rust core library match Rust: integer overflow, a shift that is too large and an index out of bounds are failures.The tool pins and where the binaries come from. Regenerating the Lean is byte-identical. Assumptions/FunsExternal.lean declares nothing. In part II, what is rewritten by hand before hax sees a function of the pinned fork.4, 7, 11
A2Lean’s kernel and its three standard axioms (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound).The axiom audit covers every theorem, and it fails when an escape hatch is planted.7
A3DyLean’s core: traces, what the attacker knows, reachability and its tactics.Its pin, the patch applied to it, the three #combine blocks that define what statements mean, and the two actions accept and receive.6
A4The hash is ideal. A digest is DyLean’s hash constructor applied to its input, as ProVerif and Tamarin treat a hash by default: two digests are equal only when their inputs are the same term, and concatenation keeps the boundary between parts. SHA-256 allows length extension and the ideal hash does not, which is irrelevant here: extension derives the digest of a longer input from a digest alone, so it matters only when part of an input is secret, and every input the verifier hashes is public or chosen by the attacker. Part II adds a second constructor, for Keccak-256, to what a term is. No cited statement mentions it; a consumer hashes its keys with it.What the reading of the hash says, against what production hashes. What the ideal hash cannot express is written down. In part II, that a path through a root is a list of whole fields and not a byte offset.5, 8

The trust chain of part I

A theorem about generated Lean says something about production only if every link below holds. Each step of the audit discharges named links, and each side-by-side panel carries a label that says how strong its link is today.

LinkWhat must holdStrength todayStep
L0The refactor made for the proof preserved production behaviour.tested the old traversal is kept and compared with the new one2
L1The files the proof sees are the files production compiles.same code included by #[path]2
L2The verification-only client behaves like production’s verifier.tested with known divergences3
L3The generated Lean means what the Rust does.assumed A14
L4The handwritten Lean readings of Rust traits are faithful.trusted5
L5The application can supply the snapshot that the theorems assume.tested for honest openings6
L6The protocol model and the way it uses DyLean are adequate.trusted6
L7The README’s claims are what the Lean statements say.trusted a reading1
L8The proofs are checked by Lean with no escape hatch.proved by the build7

The labels: proved a named Lean lemma states the link and Lean checks it. tested a test samples it. trusted a person must read both sides; nothing checks it. assumed one of A1 to A4. same code one side calls or includes the other. no link the two sides should agree and nothing relates them.

Order. Start step 7 first and let it run: it builds the toolchain and takes the longest. Then work through steps 0 to 6 in order. Steps 3, 5 and 6 are where a person’s judgement matters most. The times are rough and add up to about a day.

The trust chain of part II

Part II has the shape of a refinement. Its statements are about a Lean specification of the reader’s check, and production’s verifier, extracted unchanged, is proved to refine it. The production callers delegate to the files that the extracted crate includes, and the selectors run beside stand-in types.

LinkWhat must holdStrength todayStep
M1The production files that part II extracts mean the same in the extracted crate as in production.same code for the rules, geometry, reconstruction and layout files; trusted for claim.rs, which is compiled against stand-in types10
M2The generated Lean means what the Rust does.assumed A14, 11
M3Production’s verifier and codec delegate to the shared files without changing what they compute.tested reference tests against the code they replaced, and the conformance fixtures10, 11
M4Each extracted piece computes what the specification says at that place.proved10, 11
M5Production’s verifier, as a whole, refines RawProof.verify.proved for digests of SHA-256 width and 32-byte chunks11
M6The writer keeps what the statements assume of a snapshot.no link two examples show that the assumptions can be met9
M7The statements are combined into a guarantee about a read.no link here; it is the consumer’s proof8
M8The claims of the README and of the doc comments are what the Lean statements say.trusted a reading8
M9The proofs are checked by Lean with no escape hatch.proved by the build12

Order. Read step 0 of part I first. Then steps 8 to 12 in order; steps 9 and 11 are where a person’s judgement matters most. Part II adds about a day.

Every Lean declaration, by trust type

The trust chains say which links hold. This graph says which Lean a person has to read. It holds every Lean declaration of both parts: the handwritten definitions and theorems, the generated definitions they reach, and the three libraries under both. Lean prints the graph, and the trust type of each declaration follows from it.

  • cited statement A theorem that this guide cites, in one of three groups: inclusion, ordered reads in the model, and the model against extracted Rust. Its statement is a reading that step 1 or step 8 checks. Lean checks its proof.
  • trusted Handwritten, and a cited statement depends on what it says. Steps 5, 6 and 9 read these.
  • generated Produced from Rust by hax from the extracted crate. Assumed faithful (A1); steps 4 and 11 look at some of them.
  • assumed library DyLean (A3), the Aeneas library and hax’s core models (A1).
  • checked A lemma, or a definition that only proofs use. Lean checks it, and it is not to be read.

The rule behind the colours: start from a cited statement and follow what its statement mentions, then what the bodies of those definitions mention, and so on. Never enter a proof. Whatever is reached is what the statement says. A mistake in a checked declaration can make the build fail. It cannot change what a cited statement says.

The statements of part I and the declarations they depend on follow a fixed layout of at most 80 columns, which the build of this page enforces. Those of part II are shown as their author wrote them, at up to 100 columns.

The target has 767 declarations. 36 are statements that this guide cites: 8 for single-item inclusion, 18 for ordered reads in the model, 10 for the model against extracted Rust. What those statements say depends on 172 handwritten declarations, on 182 generated ones and on 3 libraries. The other 374 are lemmas and definitions that only proofs use: Lean checks them, and no cited statement depends on what they say.

Part I · Inclusion of one item

Steps 0 to 7. Step 7 runs the checks of both parts.

Step 0 · Primer

Read
The panel and the table below.
Pass when
You can say in one sentence what the statement in the panel assumes and what it concludes.
Links
None. This prepares steps 1 to 6.
Time
15 minutes.
LeanMeaning
RustM.ok vThe Rust code returned v. The other outcomes are a failure, which is a panic in Rust, and divergence.
Std.U64, 5#u64, x.valA u64, the literal 5, and the natural number behind x.
Slice T, s.valA Rust slice and the list behind it. A slice is shorter than usize::MAX.
[Snapshot] in a statementEverything in the class Snapshot is assumed, including its proof obligations. Read the class before the theorem.
∀ ∃ ∧ ∨ → ¬For all, there is, and, or, implies, not.
BytesA DyLean term: a literal, a concatenation or a hash. It is not a byte string.
theorem, def, class, structureA checked fact; a definition; a bundle of assumed inputs; a record.

Step 1 · What is claimed

Read
The table below, then the statements it shows: five in Inclusion.lean and two in SecurityTheorems.lean (44 lines). Statements only.
Pass when
  • Each sentence of the README says no more than the statement beside it.
  • Every hypothesis of a statement appears in the sentence, or its absence is written down.
  • You can say what the hash is in each statement and what that leaves out.
Links
L7.
Time
1 hour.

Three questions to ask of every statement. What is the hash: in every statement it is DyLean’s ideal hash, never a real one. Which inputs are trusted: the root, and in every statement also the height. What does the client have to be given before the statement applies?

Generated: each sentence is checked to occur in the README, and each statement is read from the Lean source.

The claim, and where it is madeThe Lean statement behind itReadingYour verdict
“Two openings that the extracted verifier accepts at one location under one root, for one trusted height, carry the same item and the same siblings.”
qmdb/README.md
Lean unique (statement only) Qmdb/Inclusion.lean:590–600
590theorem unique591    (h : Std.U32) (loc : Std.U64) (root : Bytes)592    (a b : Slice Std.U8) (wa wb : Slice Bytes)593    (ha :594      inclusion.verify_element_inclusion dyTerms () h loc root a wa =595        RustM.ok true)596    (hb :597      inclusion.verify_element_inclusion dyTerms () h loc root b wb =598        RustM.ok true) :599    a = b ∧600    wa = wb := by
The hash is dyTerms, DyLean's constructor. The extracted verifier is inclusion::verify_element_inclusion of the verification-only client, not production's Proof::verify_element_inclusion. Position binding is the first half of the conclusion.
“The verifier returns a verdict on every input, so it never panics or diverges, and it accepts every honest opening.”
qmdb/README.md
Lean verify_total (statement only) Qmdb/Inclusion.lean:850–854
850theorem verify_total851    (h : Std.U32) (loc : Std.U64) (root : Bytes)852    (item : Slice Std.U8) (ws : Slice Bytes) :853    ∃ b, inclusion.verify_element_inclusion dyTerms () h loc root item ws =854      RustM.ok b := by
Lean honest_opening (statement only) Qmdb/Inclusion.lean:761–769
761theorem honest_opening762    (items : Std.U64 → Slice Std.U8) (h : Std.U32)763    (bound : h.val ≤ maxHeight)764    (loc : Std.U64)765    (inside : loc.val < 2 ^ h.val) :766    inclusion.verify_element_inclusion dyTerms () h loc767      (honestRoot items h.val) (items loc)768      (honestSiblings items h.val loc bound) =769      RustM.ok true := by
verify_total: a verdict on every input, so no panic and no divergence. honest_opening: honest means built by honestRoot and honestSiblings, which are Lean definitions, not production's tree builder.
“Every acceptance that the extracted client logs on a reachable trace names the trusted snapshot height, an in-range location and the item stored there.”
qmdb/README.md
Lean client_authentication (statement only) Qmdb/SecurityTheorems.lean:31–39
31theorem client_authentication32    [Snapshot]33    (event : Acceptance) (time : Nat) :34    ∀ tr : ExecTrace,35      tr.Reachable reachability →36      tr.EventLoggedAt event time →37      event.height = Snapshot.height ∧38      event.location.val < 2 ^ event.height.val ∧39      event.item = Snapshot.items event.location := by
Stored means Snapshot.items. The property holds for every message, location and sibling list, so the trace adds no hypothesis beyond Symbolic.client_step_sound.
“Some reachable trace logs the honest acceptance of each stored item.”
qmdb/README.md
Lean honest_acceptance_logged (statement only) Qmdb/SecurityTheorems.lean:48–58
48theorem honest_acceptance_logged49    [Snapshot]50    (loc : Std.U64) (inside : loc.val < 2 ^ Snapshot.height.val) :51    ∃ tr : ExecTrace,52      tr.Reachable reachability ∧53      ∃ time,54        tr.EventLoggedAt55          ({ height := Snapshot.height,56             location := loc,57             item := Snapshot.items loc } : Acceptance)58          time := by
The trace is an attempt: the attacker sends the item, and the client runs on the siblings that the snapshot supplies. attempt_logs shows that the accepted event is in the trace. client_authentication alone does not, because a Hoare triple holds of an action that fails.
“A snapshot with a root and an accepted opening for every stored item exists at every height up to MAX_HEIGHT, the client's limit, which is production's MAX_LEAVES as a height.”
qmdb/README.md
Lean honest_snapshots_exist (statement only) Qmdb/SecurityTheorems.lean:16–24
16theorem honest_snapshots_exist17    (items : Std.U64 → Slice Std.U8) (h : Std.U32)18    (bound : h.val ≤ Inclusion.maxHeight) :19    ∃ (root : Bytes) (siblings : Std.U64 → Slice Bytes),20      ∀ loc : Std.U64,21        loc.val < 2 ^ h.val →22        inclusion.verify_element_inclusion dyTerms () h loc root (items loc)23          (siblings loc) =24          RustM.ok true :=
The assumption is not contradictory. It does not show that production's tree builder produces such a snapshot; the tests in step 6 sample that.
“The verifier accepts only heights up to MAX_HEIGHT and locations inside the tree, and it rejects an honest opening that an unused sibling follows.”
qmdb/README.md
Lean verify_bounds (statement only) Qmdb/Inclusion.lean:557–564

Lean extra_sibling_rejected (statement only) Qmdb/Inclusion.lean:774–784
774theorem extra_sibling_rejected775    (items : Std.U64 → Slice Std.U8) (h : Std.U32)776    (bound : h.val ≤ maxHeight)777    (loc : Std.U64)778    (inside : loc.val < 2 ^ h.val)779    (ws : Slice Bytes) (extra : Bytes)780    (siblings :781      ws.val = path items h.val (2 * (2 ^ h.val - 1)) 0 loc.val ++ [extra]) :782    inclusion.verify_element_inclusion dyTerms () h loc783      (honestRoot items h.val) (items loc) ws =784      RustM.ok false := by
verify_bounds: acceptance implies h ≤ maxHeight and an in-range location. extra_sibling_rejected: one unused sibling after the honest ones.

No theorem is stated twice. The properties of the verifier are stated in Inclusion.lean, and the two results about the protocol and its assumption in SecurityTheorems.lean. The table of trusted declarations says which definitions each of the eight statements depends on.

Step 2 · Production code and the refactor

Read
terms.rs (109 lines) and traversal.rs (165 lines) in full. Then the changes to hasher.rs Diff and proof.rs Diff against the baseline.
Pass when
  • The refactor preserves behaviour: the old traversal and the new one agree wherever production calls them.
  • The two shared files name nothing from the crate around them, so they mean the same in both crates.
  • You have a list of the production code paths that do not go through the shared files.
Links
L0, L1.
Time
1.5 hours.

The proof needed production to be split. Hash inputs moved into terms.rs, as lists of parts over an abstract hash. The recursive traversal moved into traversal.rs, behind three small traits. Production reaches both through thin wrappers. The change is 486 added and 28 removed lines in four files. The last of them belong to part II: current_root in terms.rs and hash_parts in hasher.rs.

The crate that hax extracts includes the two files by path, so L1 holds by construction: lib.rs has one #[path] line for each. What a person checks is that neither file has a use of its surroundings, which would resolve differently in the two crates.

The regression test covers both tree families and both bagging policies, every range of trees with 1 to 16 leaves, with and without node collection, and three kinds of damaged input. It compares one peak at a time.

Diff compares this checkout’s file against the original baseline b45ef2d78, including test changes in the same file. New files have an empty left pane. Install the local VS Code handler with python3 verification/qmdb/code-diff.py --install.

Step 3 · The verification-only client

Read
inclusion.rs (105 lines) and geometry.rs against production’s verifier in proof.rs, mmr/mod.rs and qmdb/mod.rs. Then inclusion/tests.rs.
Pass when
  • Every line of verify has a production counterpart or a divergence that you have written down.
  • For each divergence you can say whether the tests cover it.
  • You can say which deployed configuration the client models.
Links
L2.
Time
2 hours.

The theorems are about inclusion::verify_element_inclusion and inclusion::accept_inclusion. Production never calls either. They are an entry point written for the proof. It calls production’s own range-proof reconstruction, reconstruct::reconstruct, over production’s MMR geometry and QMDB’s bagging, with one item, one peak and a trusted tree size. Production’s reconstruct_root_inner calls the same function with the hasher’s byte encodings and with the sizes the proof carries. So the theorems reach production’s Proof::verify_element_inclusion only as far as the two calls return the same verdict, and that is shown by tests.

What the differential tests vary

Both tests build production trees with SHA-256 and compare against the client over the test-only hasher Concrete.

InputVariedNever varied
Tree sizePowers of two: heights 0 to 6 for verdicts, 0 to 8 for honest openings.Sizes that are not a power of two, which the client cannot express. Heights above 8, except that 63 and u32::MAX are rejected.
ItemRandom bytes, 0 to 39 long. One claim appends a zero byte.An item that is itself a hash input of a node.
LocationEvery location; the next location with the same item; the first location out of range.Locations far out of range.
SiblingsHonest; one appended; the last one dropped; each one replaced in turn; the first two swapped.More than one change at once.
RootHonest; one unrelated digest.The root of a tree of another size or bagging.
Proof fieldsNone.leaves is always the proof’s own and inactive_peaks is always 0.
Height given to the clientNone.It is always the true height of the tree.
HasherNone.Production side: SHA-256 with backward-fold bagging, which is QMDB’s. Client side: Concrete.

Step 4 · Extraction, time-boxed

Read
The four panels below, for plausibility only.
Pass when
  • Each generated definition has the shape of its Rust: the same branches in the same order, and a possible failure at every arithmetic step.
  • The checks of step 7 confirm that the generated files are reproducible and that nothing was added by hand.
Links
L3 stays assumed.
Time
30 minutes. Stop there.

This step does not establish that the translation is right. That is assumption A1. Its purpose is to let you recognise the generated code that the statements in steps 1, 5 and 6 mention, and to notice a gross mismatch.

Lean does not reason about the generated code directly. The proofs first show that each generated encoding function returns one named term. From there on, statements talk about those terms.

The index at the end lists every generated Merkle definition with its Rust source.

Step 5 · Trusted readings

Read
In Terms.lean the definitions part, chain, dyTerms, toByteArray, toSlice and messages.
Pass when
  • For each panel, the Lean on the right is a fair account of the Rust on the left, or you have written down where it is not and whether a statement depends on it.
  • You accept the ideal hash for the question you are asking, or you have written down why not.
Links
L4, A4.
Time
1 hour.

The generated code is generic in the hash. A theorem needs a concrete thing to put in that place, and a person wrote it: dyTerms. Every statement of step 1 uses it. It makes the hash a constructor of terms, the usual choice of symbolic tools. That is the largest assumption of this proof, because it is what turns “the same root” into “the same tree”.

Step 6 · Assumption and protocol

Read
Assumptions.lean (41 lines). In Protocol.lean the definition of client. In Client.lean the definitions accept and receive. The patch.
Pass when
  • The snapshot is something an application has, and you can say what it does not tie down.
  • The attacker chooses the message, the location and the siblings without restriction.
  • Nothing in the model lets the client refuse to act where the Rust would act.
  • The patch adds no axiom, and you have read the one definition it adds.

Part II · Ordered reads under a checkpoint root

Steps 8 to 12. A reader holds a root that it trusts and receives a claim about one key with a proof: the key has this value, or the key has none. Part II is about when such a claim can be believed. Its root is the canonical root of a current database over an MMB, in the format of Commonware v2026.11.0. Tempo pins that code through klkvr/monorepo 69cc03365, upstream v2026.11.0 plus one commit to partitioned ordered navigation, and this branch carries it.

A specification and a refinement. The main statements of part II are about RawProof.verify, a Lean definition of the reader's check. Step 11 proves that production's verifier, extracted unchanged, refines it: whatever production accepts, the definition accepts. So the soundness statements hold of production's verifier. The definitions of step 9 are a specification that Lean checks against the Rust, not a trusted model; the structures that describe the database behind the root stay assumptions.

Which structure is assumed: none, an Active.Snapshot, an Ordered.Snapshot, a Layout? Does extracted Rust occur in it?

From a proof to a read

No theorem of this repository chains the statements above (M7). A consumer’s argument has to go through these rows, and the last column is what each row asks for.

Step of the argumentStatementWhat it needs
The checkpoint digest gives two roots, in order.rootPair_bindingThat the digest is authentic, and which root answers which query. Neither is stated here.
Production's ordered client accepts the claim's operation under a root, with the leaf count and the inactive-peak count that the proof carries.verify_selected_sound, verify_operation_refinesA 32-byte chunk, digests of SHA-256 width, and fixed-width keys and values.
Those counts are the database’s.verify_operation_header, Header.bindingA header of the database with the same root: Database.root_eq and count_eq.
The proof is two openings at the planner’s paths.verify_operation_sound, RawProof.soundNothing more.
They are openings of the snapshot.Mmb.acceptedA Layout of the snapshot at that inactive-peak count.
The opened operation is live and is the one stored there.Active.acceptedAn Active.Snapshot.
The claim selects that operation.accepts_iff, with the checked lemma verifyWith_monoNothing.
The claim equals the replayed state.accepted_readAn Ordered.Snapshot and an injective encoding, such as Layout.encoding.

Ordered.Database bundles the structures of the last column, and the two examples build one. That the pieces fit is therefore shown for one leaf and for three, by empty_claim and singleton_claims.

Step 9 · The specification and what it assumes

Read
Plan.lean in full. In Raw.lean the definitions up to RawProof.verify. The structures Snapshot in Active.lean and Ordered.lean and Layout in Mmb.lean. Journal.lean up to replay.
Pass when
  • You can explain each check of fieldsValid and each case of envelope.
  • For each proof field of the three structures you can say what in the writer keeps it true, or you have written down that you do not know.
  • You accept replay as the meaning of a read.
Links
M6. The definitions read here are the right-hand sides of M4 and M5.
Time
3 hours.

Two kinds of definition matter. The verifier and its plan say what a reader checks; step 11 proves that production computes them, so an error there would make a refinement theorem fail to build. The three structures say what is assumed of the database behind the root, and nothing ties them to Rust: the second table of trusted declarations lists them.

Step 10 · Production code shared with part II

Read
claim.rs, activity.rs, cyclic.rs, current_root in terms.rs and layout.rs. Then reads.rs and, in Extraction.lean, the readings keys, readOp and select.
Pass when
  • Every name that claim.rs takes from its surroundings has a stand-in that behaves like production’s for the two selectors.
  • You can say what accepts_iff leaves out.
  • You accept the byte-list writer of Encoding.lean as a reading of production's codec buffer.
Links
M1, M4.
Time
1.5 hours.

Production was changed so that its pieces could be shared with the proof. The two selectors moved out of the verify methods of the ordered proofs into claim.rs. The bit test moved into activity.rs, the decision of contains_cyclic into cyclic.rs, the preimage of the canonical root into terms.rs, and the field order, tags and padding of encoded operations into layout.rs. Each production caller delegates to these files, and the symbolic crate includes them by #[path].

Step 11 · The extracted verifier against the plan

Read
rules.rs and grafting/rules.rs in full, reconstruct in reconstruct.rs, and the statements of Extracted.lean and Reads.lean.
Pass when
  • You can say which production function each statement is about and that it is included unchanged.
  • You accept the two hypotheses of verify_operation_refines: digests of SHA-256 width and a 32-byte chunk.
  • You can name the production checks that the refinement relies on: chunk size, coverage, graftable count, the two suffix checks, the digest count, element exhaustion and the root comparison.
Links
M2, M3, M4, M5.
Time
2 hours.

Production's OperationProof::verify builds the fields of the proof and calls rules::verify_operation with the MMB geometry and QMDB's bagging. That function, the range-proof reconstruction it calls, the MMB geometry and the grafting rules are extracted unchanged. The panels below follow the proof: the peaks of the tree, the traversal of the peak that holds the location, where a chunk enters, the bagging, and the refinement that combines them. The last panel is the ordered client, which encodes the selected operation with layout.rs and calls the same verifier.

Step 12 · Machine evidence of part II

Read
CheckpointAudit.lean and the part II entries of mutations.toml.
Pass when
  • The audit of part II names the namespaces of its statements and reports only standard axioms.
  • You can say what the extraction check of step 7 covers for part II.
Links
M9.
Time
30 minutes.
ProbeRecorded outcomeShows
(cd verification/lean && lake build Qmdb.CheckpointAudit)Every theorem in [Qmdb.Active, Qmdb.CurrentRoot, Qmdb.Mmb, Qmdb.Ordered, Commonware.Symbolic] depends only on standard axioms.No proof of part II uses sorry, native evaluation or an added axiom. The audit goes by namespace, as in part I.
bash verification/check.shThe extraction matches the committed files, which include rules.rs, grafting/rules.rs, reconstruct.rs, the MMB geometry and layout.rs.The Lean that part II's theorems are about is what hax produces from the production files of this branch.

Eight mutations of mutations.toml change the files of part II: the activity check, the partial-chunk check, the zero-chunk graft, the graftable count, the update tag, the MMB child positions, the MMB peak heights and the backward fold. Each breaks a named module: Qmdb.Mmb.Extracted, Qmdb.Ordered.Encoding, Qmdb.Mmb.ChildGeometry, Qmdb.Mmb.Peaks or Qmdb.Reconstruct.

Residual risks

What remains after every step passes. Each is a property of the approach or a gap. R1 to R7 belong to part I and R8 to R13 to part II. None is a flaw in a proof, and no independent reviewer has gone through either part.

#RiskLinkWhat would close it
R1The translation from Rust to Lean is wrong in a way that changes what the verifier means.L3An audit of hax, Charon, Aeneas and their library models, or a second extraction route that agrees.
R2The proved call is not the deployed one. Both run production’s reconstruct::reconstruct, but the client fixes one item of a tree with one peak and a trusted size and hashes through symbolic terms, while production hashes bytes. Tests on trees of up to 64 leaves tie the two verdicts.L2State the theorems for any leaf and inactive count, which the reconstruction lemmas already allow, and prove production’s byte terms an instance of the symbolic ones.
R3The modelled root is a QMDB operations root over an MMR. A QMDB over the MMB family, whose roots carry another domain byte and other peaks, is covered by part II only.L2Run the client over geometry::Mmb. The reconstruction lemmas hold for any geometry; the peaks of an MMB need their own Yields lemma.
R4The tree size is trusted. Production reads leaves and inactive_peaks from the proof, which the attacker writes, and relies on the root committing to them. No statement covers that, and the tests never vary them.L2A statement in which the size comes from the proof and the root alone is trusted. Part II has one: verify_operation_header with Header.binding. Part I’s client is unchanged.
R5The hash is ideal. No statement reduces a broken opening to a collision of a real hash, and facts about bytes are outside the model: in bytes the root of a small tree is also a leaf digest, and only positions keep a long item apart from a node.L4, A4An argument over production’s bytes beside the symbolic one. This branch had a reduction to an explicit collision and dropped it for a smaller trusted base.
R6Honest roots are built by code that the proof does not see. The tree builder hashes nodes through a second encoding, and the journal chooses what is stored at each location.L5Route the builder through the part lists of terms.rs; state the snapshot in terms of the journal.
R7The toolchain is pinned by name, not by content: the hax binary and the dependency builds are whatever is on the machine, and no CI runs the check.L8Record how the binary is built, hash it, and run check.sh in CI.
R8The refinement has two hypotheses. Every supplied digest has the width of SHA-256, which production’s digest type guarantees and the symbolic digests do not. The bitmap chunk has 32 bytes, as Plan fixes 256 bits; production accepts any chunk whose bit width is a power of two.M5Generalize Plan over the chunk width, or state that every deployment uses 32-byte chunks.
R9The proved code is this branch’s. Production was changed to delegate to the extracted rules files, and Tempo’s pin does not contain those changes. Reference tests and conformance fixtures tie the two, and they are not a proof.M3Upstream the rules files, so that a Tempo pin contains them.
R10Nothing ties the writer to the assumed snapshot. The activity bits, the successor links, the commit floor and the layout of the root are hypotheses, shown to be satisfiable for one leaf and for three.M6A model or an extraction of the writer with the invariants proved, or tests that check them on production databases of many sizes.
R11The statements are not combined here. A guarantee about a read needs the rows of step 8 chained, and a statement about checkpoints: who authenticates the pair of roots and which root answers which query.M7Audit the consumer’s proof, or state the composed theorem in this repository.
R12The ordered client is a verification-only entry point. It calls production’s selectors, layout and verifier with stand-in types, and production’s KeyValueProof::verify and ExclusionProof::verify are not extracted themselves. Differential tests compare the client’s verdicts with theirs on databases of up to 450 keys, honest proofs and altered ones.M1Extract the ordered proof methods, or route them through the client’s functions.
R13The writer that the encoding runs with is a reading: its primitive appends stand for production’s codec buffer, and the codec of keys and values is assumed fixed-width and injective. A path through a root is still a list of whole fields, as in R5.M4, A4Extract the codec’s writer, or test bytes against encoded operations.
